{{Short description|Anglican priest and academic in Ireland in the second half of the 17th century}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2022}}
{{Use Hiberno-English|date=January 2022}}
'''Milo Sumner,''' ( – 21 March 1686) [[Doctor of Divinity|D.D.]] also known as '''Miles Symner''', '''Miles Symmes''' or '''Myles Symner''', was an [[Anglican]] priest and academic in [[Ireland]] in the second half of the seventeenth century.<ref>"The Works of Jonathan Swift: Memoirs of Jonathan Swift, D. D" Scott, W (Ed) p&nbsp;44: Edinburgh Archibald, Constable & Co; 1814</ref>

Sumner was educated at [[Trinity College, Dublin]], where he was a scholar in 1626.<ref>"Alumni Dublinenses: a register of the students, graduates, professors and provosts of Trinity College in the University of Dublin (1593–1860)" Burtchaell, George Dames/Sadleir, Thomas Ulick (Eds) p&nbsp;793: Dublin, Alex Thom and Co, 1935</ref> He was a major in the Parliamentary Army in the [[English Civil War|Civil War]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Webb |first=D.A. |editor-first=Barlett |editor-last=J.R.|date=1992 |title=Trinity College Dublin Record Volume 1991 |location=Dublin |publisher=Trinity College Dublin Press |isbn=1-871408-07-5|page=}}</ref><ref name=400Hist>{{cite web |url= https://www.maths.tcd.ie/about/400Hist/5.php |title=400 years of mathematics: MYLES SYMNER and the new learning |first=T. D. |last=Spearman |date=1992 |publisher=Trinity College Dublin |access-date=26 September 2022}}</ref> He was appointed Fellow and Professor of Mathematics by the Parliamentary Commissioners in 1652, a position which became the [[Donegall Lectureship at Trinity College Dublin|Donegall Lectureship]]. He became [[Archdeacon of Clogher]] in 1661 and then [[Archdeacon of Kildare]] from 1668.<ref>"Fasti Ecclesiae Hibernicae: The succession of the prelates Volume 3" p&nbsp;91 [[Henry Cotton (divine)|Cotton, H.]] [[Dublin]], Hodges & Smith, 1848–1878</ref>
